implementation_notes: The JDK already ships the combinator on the interface: `Function<T,R>.andThen(Function<? super R,? extends V>)` and `.compose(...)` are default methods, and `Function.identity()` provides the identity element (docs.oracle.com). Primitive specializations (UnaryOperator, IntUnaryOperator) and the stream/Optional operations (Stream.map, Optional.map/flatMap) reuse the same notion of sequential application, so nothing of the classic structure is left to write. A hand-written combinator is only needed for arities the JDK does not cover (BiFunction composition) or to add error accumulation, which is a different pattern.
pitfalls: andThen reads left-to-right and compose reads right-to-left; mixing the two in one chain is the classic silent reversal (the javadoc says compose applies before this function, andThen after).
Wildcard capture makes long chains compile only with explicit type witnesses or a cast at the join, because each andThen widens the type variables.
andThen allocates a new lambda capturing both functions on every call; build the composed Function once and store it instead of recomposing per item.
